children: The details of the October inflation data are uglier than the topline figures suggest, Glenmede's Jason Pride says in a note. Energy inflation decelerated sharply to 0.7% after a 5.2% surge in September, meaning the price increases for October were more heavily driven by parts of the inflation basket, such as rent and healthcare, that the Federal Reserve can't overlook as one-off shocks, Pride says. Core inflation has been running at an annualized pace approaching 4% for the past three months, which is not the trajectory of an index that's moving toward the Fed's 2% inflation target, he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)
